chapters.intro: Dutch is mostly written the way it sounds, so once you know the handful of tricky sounds below you can read almost any word out loud. Tap 🔊 to hear each example, repeat it, and don't worry about a perfect accent.

sections.title: De g en ch (the scrapey sound)
sections.note: g and ch make the same rough sound from the back of the throat, a bit like clearing it. In the south it's softer.

items.en: to go — the classic hard g
to laugh — ch is the same sound
gladly — two g sounds in one word

sections.title: De ui, eu en oe
sections.note: Three vowel sounds with no English match. ui is rounded like oy with pursed lips; eu is like the u in the French peur; oe sounds like the English oo in boot.

items.en: book — the oe sounds like oo

sections.title: De ij en ei (they sound the same)
sections.note: ij and ei sound identical, like the y in my. Spelling just has to be learned per word: lange ij vs korte ei.

sections.title: De au en ou (also the same)
sections.note: au and ou sound the same too, like the ow in now. Again, only the spelling differs per word.

sections.title: De stille e (the schwa)
sections.note: An unstressed e at the end of a word or in a small word sounds like a soft uh, never a sharp e. It's the most common vowel sound in Dutch.

items.en: to walk — the e is a soft uh

sections.title: Long vs short vowels & the doubling rule
sections.body: A single vowel in a closed syllable (ending in a consonant) is short: man, bos, pit. To keep a vowel LONG, you either double the vowel or open the syllable. So when a word gets an ending, the spelling shifts to protect the sound. Double the consonant to keep a vowel short: man becomes mannen (still short a). Drop one vowel when the syllable opens to keep it long: boom becomes bomen, maan becomes manen (still long aa, now spelled with one a). Rule of thumb: short vowel plus ending equals double consonant; long vowel plus ending equals single vowel in an open syllable.

sections.title: Klemtoon (word stress)
sections.body: Most Dutch words stress the first syllable: TA-fel, WIN-kel, MOE-der. But words starting with the prefixes ge-, be-, ver- and ont- usually stress the next syllable: geLUK, beTAlen, verSTAAN, ontMOEten. Loanwords often keep their own stress, like resTAUrant. Putting the stress on the right syllable matters more for being understood than getting every sound perfect.

sections.title: Hoe spel je dat? (spelling out loud)
sections.note: You'll need this at every counter and on the phone. Practise spelling your own name and address.

items.nl: Mijn naam is Anna, A N N A.

sections.q: Welk woord heeft dezelfde klank als ijs?
sections.qEn: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'ijs' (ice)?
sections.explanation: ij and ei sound exactly the same, so 'ijs' and 'klein' rhyme. 'huis' has the ui sound and 'boek' has the oe sound.

chapters.intro: Core everyday nouns for your body, your family and describing people. Learn each noun together with its de or het, and tap 🔊 to hear it.

sections.title: Learn de or het with every word
sections.body: Each noun is a de-word or a het-word, and there's no reliable rule, so always memorise the article with the noun. The lists below already show it for you. Tip: most body parts and family members are de-words.

sections.title: Talking about aches
sections.body: At the doctor you'll often add pijn (pain). Say ik heb pijn in mijn ... plus the body part: ik heb pijn in mijn buik (I have a stomach ache), ik heb keelpijn (I have a sore throat), ik heb hoofdpijn (I have a headache).

sections.title: Family shortcuts
sections.body: de ouders means the parents and de kinderen means the children (an irregular plural). Informally many people say mama and papa, just like in English. Your partner's parents are your schoonouders (parents-in-law).

sections.title: Mensen beschrijven (describing people)
sections.note: Use these with the verb zijn: hij is jong, zij is vriendelijk.

items.nl: Hoeveel broers en zussen heb je?
items.en: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

sections.qEn: Fill in the gap: 'This is ... father' (my father).
sections.explanation: mijn means 'my'. 'het' or 'een' would just mean 'the' or 'a' father, which doesn't fit 'this is ... father'.

chapters.titleNl: Woorden: eten, kleding, kleuren, huis & dieren
chapters.titleEn: Words: food, clothes, colours, house & animals
chapters.intro: The everyday vocabulary you'll meet at the supermarket, in the wardrobe and around the home. Learn each noun with its de or het, and tap 🔊 to hear it.

sections.title: At the shop
sections.body: To ask for things, use ik wil graag ... (I'd like ...) or mag ik ... (may I have ...). For amounts: een kilo appels (a kilo of apples), een liter melk (a litre of milk), een stuk kaas (a piece of cheese). De boodschappen means the groceries.

sections.title: De kleuren (colours)
sections.note: Colours work like adjectives: de rode jas, het groene boek. Most add an -e before a noun.

sections.title: One word, two meanings
sections.body: Watch out for de bank: it means both the sofa and the bank where you keep money. Context makes it clear. And het toilet is a common alternative to de wc.

sections.title: De dieren (animals)
sections.note: de poes and de kat both mean cat; poes is the cosier, everyday word.

sections.explanation: slaapkamer literally means sleep-room (bedroom). slaap comes from slapen, to sleep. The kitchen is for cooking and the bathroom for washing.
